For fixed source item i, log-lift equals log(1+c_ij/(αq_j)) + log(α/(n_i+α)); therefore candidate ranking depends only on c_ij/q_j. This algebraic implication means increasing α cannot change single-row rankings before clipping. A singleton targeting a sufficiently unpopular item can outrank a well-supported edge. Monotone clipping caps magnitude or creates ties; it does not establish statistical reliability. Row constants still matter when aggregating multiple history items, especially after nonlinear clipping.

Explicit support protection could use minimum distinct-user support or c_ij/(c_ij+λ) times positive log-lift; these are tunable heuristics, not calibrated evidence. A Bayesian alternative uses the marginal posterior p_ij ~ Beta(c_ij+αq_j, n_i−c_ij+α(1−q_j)): require Pr(p_ij>q_j | data)>τ, or rank by a conservative posterior quantile of log(p_ij/q_j). These are proposed adaptations assuming fixed q_j; estimated background uncertainty and repeated-user dependence need care. Variance-standardized posterior log-odds provides another evidence-sensitive approach, following [Monroe et al.](https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/myl/Monroe.pdf), although log-odds and log-lift are different statistics.

Useful baselines: popularity; first-order Markov probabilities, which rank next-item likelihood rather than enrichment over popularity; sequential rules, which aggregate ordered pair evidence with distance/history weighting; and V-SKNN, which retrieves similar sessions using position-weighted session representations. [Ludewig et al.](https://d-nb.info/1222824833/34) found simple rules and neighborhood methods competitive across session datasets; this does not establish their ranking on Amazon histories. Compare these alongside raw and support-weighted lift using the prescribed macro validation HR@10, fitting counts and popularity exclusively from training interactions.
